title: The Seeing-Nature Is Unmoving
author: Annotated by Mingde
excerpt: At that time the World-Honored One stretched forth his hand — soft as cotton, adorned with the marks of the net and of the wheel, and radiant — opened his five fingers, and instructed and admonished Ananda and the great assembly: "When I first attained the Way, in the Deer Garden, I said to Kaundinya and the five monks and to the four assemblies of you: 'All beings fail to attain bodhi and arhatship because they are misled by the defilements of guest-dust.' At that time, because of what did you awaken, that you have now attained the holy fruit?

inline.s: [At that time the World-Honored One stretched forth his hand — soft as cotton, adorned with the net-mark and the wheel-mark, and radiant — opened his fingers of five wheels, and instructed and admonished Ananda and the great assembly: "When I first attained the Way, in the Deer Garden, I said to Kaundinya and the five monks and to the four assemblies of you: 'All beings fail to attain bodhi and arhatship because they are misled and led astray by the defilements of guest-dust.' At that time, because of what did you awaken, that you have now attained the holy fruit?"]

At that time, the World-Honored One stretched out his hand — fine and soft as cotton, bearing the mark of the thousand-spoked net, and emitting golden light — and opened his fingers of five wheels to instruct and admonish Ananda and the great assembly: "When I first attained the Way, in the Deer Park, I preached to Kaundinya and the five monks, and to the four assemblies of you: 'All beings are unable to accomplish the supreme bodhi and arhatship; it is because they are misled by the defilements of guest-dust.' At that time, because of what were you awakened, that you have now become arhats?"

[Cotton (toulo mian)]A kind of cotton, fine as flower-floss. [The cotton hand]One of the Buddha's eighty marks of excellence — that his hands and feet are soft and supple as cotton. [The fingers of wheels]The fingers of the Buddha all bear the pattern of the thousand-spoked wheel, hence they are called the fingers of the wheel. [The Deer Garden]The Deer Park (Migadāya), in Vārāṇasī of central India; after his awakening the Buddha came here to preach the four noble truths and to deliver Kaundinya and the five monks. [Ājñāta (A raṇya dō)]That is, Kaundinya. A-raṇya-dō is the given name; Kaundinya is the family name. [The four assemblies]Monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. [Upāsaka]Rendered in Chinese as "pure-faith man" — a male lay devotee who, living at home, draws near to and serves the three jewels and upholds the five precepts. [Upāsikā]Rendered in Chinese as "pure-faith woman" — a female lay devotee who, living at home, draws near to and serves the three jewels and upholds the five precepts. [The four noble truths]The truth of suffering, the truth of its arising, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the "truth of suffering" sets forth the truth that life is full of suffering. Second, the "arising" in the "truth of its arising" means bringing about and causing; it sets forth the truth of how the suffering of life comes about. The suffering of life arises from craving, and then attachment, and then the creating of karma, and then suffering, and then the round of birth and death. Third, the "truth of cessation" sets forth the truth of stilling all suffering. When all the aggregations of suffering (craving) are forever cut off without remainder, without grasping or attachment, one no longer creates karma, suffers, or transmigrates — this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the "truth of the path" sets forth how one forever puts an end to the aggregates of suffering (craving), that is, the path to the extinction of suffering. Of the four noble truths, arising is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit.

[At that time Kaundinya rose from his seat and said to the Buddha: "I am now an elder, and alone among the great assembly have obtained the name of the one who understood, because I awakened to the two words 'guest' and 'dust' and so attained the fruit. World-Honored One! Consider a wayfarer who lodges at an inn, either to stop for the night or to take a meal; when lodging and eating are finished, he dresses his pack
chù

and presses onward, having no leisure to settle. If he were indeed the owner, he would naturally have nowhere to go. Thinking in this way, I understood: not staying is called the guest; staying is called the master. 'Not staying' is the meaning of guest. Again, like a sky newly cleared of clouds — when the bright sun rises and its light enters through a crevice, it reveals all the forms of dust in the air. The substance of the dust moves and sways, while empty space remains still. Thinking in this way, I understood: clear and still is called space; moving and swaying is called dust. 'Moving' is the meaning of dust." The Buddha said: "So it is."]

At that time Kaundinya rose and said to the Buddha: "I am now an elder, and alone among the great assembly have obtained the name of the one who understood, because I awakened to the two words 'guest' and 'dust' and so attained the fruit. World-Honored One! Consider a wayfarer who lodges at an inn, either to stop for the night or to take a meal; when lodging and eating are finished, he packs his baggage and goes on ahead, without leisure to settle. If he were truly the innkeeper, of course he would not pack up and set out. Then I reflected thus: not staying is called the guest; staying is called the master. The meaning of 'guest' is coming and going. Again, when the sky clears and the bright sun rises, the sunlight passes through the cracks of doors and windows and reveals the dust in the air. These specks of dust sway and move, while empty space remains still and unmoving. Then I reflected thus: clear and still is called space; moving and swaying is called dust. The meaning of 'dust' is swaying and moving." The Buddha confirmed: "So it is."

[Alone obtained the name of the one who understood]When the Buddha was preaching in the Deer Park, he asked the monks: "Did you understand?" Only Kaundinya answered: "I understood." [The sky has cleared (jì
jì
)]When rain and snow have stopped and the sky brightens. [The sun (yáng) rises]
yáng
)]The sun rises.

Above, Kaundinya relates the course of his realization of the Way. In it, the master and empty space are metaphors for the true mind (profound, still, and unmoving); the guest is a metaphor for the coarse and heavy defilements (the thoughts that come and go); the dust is a metaphor for the subtle defilements (the thoughts that rise and fall lightly). The bright sun rising into the sky is a metaphor for the radiance of self-nature breaking forth, for only then can one see clearly the subtle defilements. Once one has realized the deep meaning of master and guest, space and dust, one has an entry point for practice.

[At once the Tathāgata, in the midst of the great assembly, curled his fingers of five wheels into a fist, and having curled them opened them again; having opened them, curled them once more, and said to Ananda: "What do you now see?" Ananda said: "I see the Tathāgata's palm of a hundred treasures, in the midst of the assembly, opening and closing." The Buddha told Ananda: "You see my hand, in the midst of the assembly, opening and closing — is it that my hand has opening and closing? Or is it that your seeing has opening and closing?" Ananda said: "The World-Honored One's precious hand, in the midst of the assembly, opens and closes; I see the Tathāgata's hand itself opening and closing. It is not that my seeing-nature has opening and closing." The Buddha said: "Who moves? Who is still?" Ananda said: "The Buddha's hand does not stay; but as to my seeing-nature, there is not yet even stillness — who is there that is without staying?" The Buddha said: "So it is."]

At once, the Tathāgata, in the midst of the great assembly, curled his fingers of five wheels into a fist; having curled them he opened them, and having opened them curled them into a fist again, and said to Ananda: "What do you now see?" Ananda said: "I see the Tathāgata's palm of a hundred treasures, opening and closing in the midst of the assembly." The Buddha told Ananda: "You see my hand opening and closing in the midst of the assembly — after all, is it my hand that has opening and closing? Or is it your seeing that has opening and closing?" Ananda said: "The World-Honored One's precious hand opens and closes in the midst of the assembly. I see that the Tathāgata's hand itself opens and closes; it is not that my seeing-nature has opening and closing." The Buddha said: "Who moves? Who is still?" Ananda said: "The Buddha's hand opens and closes without staying, but as to my seeing-nature, there is not even stillness — how much less is there movement!" The Buddha confirmed: "So it is."

[And as to my seeing-nature, there is not even stillness]This is Ananda's realization that his seeing-nature is not only without movement but also without stillness — that both movement and stillness are left behind.

[The Tathāgata then, from his wheel-palm, sent forth a beam of precious light, alighting to the right of Ananda; at once Ananda turned his head and looked right. Again he sent forth a beam of light, alighting to the left of Ananda, and Ananda again turned his head and looked left. The Buddha told Ananda: "Why does your head move today?" Ananda said: "I see the Tathāgata sending forth wondrous precious light that comes to my left and my right; therefore I look left and look right, and my head moves of itself." The Buddha said: "Ananda, when you gaze at the Buddha's light and turn your head left and right, is it your head that moves? Or is it your seeing that moves?" Ananda said: "World-Honored One! It is my head that moves; but as to my seeing-nature, there is not yet even a stopping — who is there that moves?" The Buddha said: "So it is."]

The Buddha then, from his wheel-palm, sent forth a beam of precious light that fell to the right of Ananda's body; at once Ananda turned his head to look right. The Buddha again sent forth a beam of light that fell to the left of Ananda's body, and Ananda turned his head to look left. The Buddha told Ananda: "Why does your head move now?" Ananda said: "I see the Tathāgata letting forth wondrous precious light that now comes to my left, now to my right; so I turn left, turn right, to look at it, and my head naturally moves." The Buddha said: "Ananda, when you gaze at the Buddha's light and turn your head left and right, is it your head that moves, after all? Or is it your seeing that moves?" Ananda said: "World-Honored One! It is my head that moves; but as to my seeing-nature, there is not yet even a stopping — how much less is there any movement!" The Buddha said, confirming: "So it is."

[Thereupon the Tathāgata proclaimed to the whole assembly: If beings call that which sways and moves "dust," and that which does not stay "guest" — then you observe Ananda's head moving of itself, while the seeing is unmoved; and again you observe my hand itself opening and closing, while the seeing is without unrolling or folding.]

Thereupon, the Buddha proclaimed to the whole assembly: "If beings call that which sways and moves 'dust,' and that which does not stay 'guest' — then you see Ananda's head moving of itself, while your seeing is not at all moved; and again you see my hand itself opening and closing, while your seeing is without unrolling or folding."

[Why do you now take the moving as your body? And take the moving as your realm? From beginning to end, thought after thought arises and passes away, and you lose the true nature and act in inversion. The nature-mind being lost and true, you mistake objects for yourself, and circling within this, you take up the flow of transmigration.]

Why do you to this very day take the moving (birth, aging, sickness, death) as the body? And take the moving (becoming, enduring, decaying, vanishing) as the realm? Then from beginning to end, at every moment false thoughts flutter in profusion (thought after thought arises and passes away), and you lose the true nature (this profound, still, unmoving true nature is the very self), and act in inversion (mistaking the five aggregates body-and-mind for the self, and the clamorous dust-realms for the real). When the nature-mind is lost (the true mind is transformed into the false mind),
you take the physical body as your own body and the shadowy reflections of the six sense-fields as your own mind, and so within transmigration you bring on your own flowing around.
[From beginning to end]From the start to the finish. Jì
jì

): to reach, and. [The five aggregates]The aggregate of form, of feeling, of thought, of volitional formations, and of consciousness — the five great factors that compose body and mind. Of these, the aggregate of form composes the body, and the remaining four aggregates compose the mind.

[The nature-mind]The true mind. [Mistaking objects for oneself]Taking the physical body as one's own body and the shadowy reflections of the six sense-fields as one's own mind. The Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra says:

"What is ignorance? Good man! All beings, from the beginningless past, are in all manner of inversion, like a lost man who changes the four directions about, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of his own body and the shadowy reflections of the six sense-fields as the mark of his own mind. It is like a man with diseased eyes who sees blossoms in empty space and a second moon. Good man! In space there are in truth no blossoms; it is the sick man's false clinging. Because of this false clinging, not only is he deluded about the self-nature of empty space, he is also deluded about the place whence the real blossoms arise. Because of this false existence, he turns round in birth and death — and this is called ignorance."
(For the annotated explanation see
A Detailed Explanation of the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra

) [The four great elements]Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has heat as its nature, wind has movement as its nature. All the material things in the world have the four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called "great." Here the four great elements refer to the body. [The shadowy reflections of the six sense-fields]The various imaginings that the six sense-organs produce when they take hold of the six sense-fields — and these imaginings are all false and unreal; hence they are called the shadowy reflections of the six sense-fields — the illusion that arises from conditions of the six sense-fields.
